newsitem.title: GERMANY: German upper house urges EMU discipline.
newsitem.headline: German upper house urges EMU discipline.

text.p: Germany's upper house of parliament on Friday urged strict discipline in the European economic and monetary union (EMU) and said it must be consulted on how sanctions will be imposed against members with excessive deficits.
The upper house, which represents Germany's 16 federal states, said this consultation was necessary to ensure states maintained their traditional budgetary autonomy.

"The upper house stressed its view that a precondition for a successful EMU is strict and narrow adherence to the convergence criteria set down in the Maastricht Treaty," the chamber said in a statement.
EMU must be based on long-term stability and growth to prevent dangers of rising inflation, higher interest rates, increased unemployment and internal tensions, it said.
European Central Bank independence is also an indispensable element, it added.
The upper house stressed that national law would govern how states apply European Union (EU) guidelines on the debt and deficit criteria for EMU.

Before the vote, Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber accused the Social Democrats (SPD), who control the upper house but are in opposition in the lower house, of wanting to water down the Maastricht criteria for joining EMU in 1999.

"Because the EU will not have a common economic and financial policy in the foreseeable future, the Maastricht criteria are the decisive measuring sticks for sufficient convergence between member states," he said.

Stoiber, one of the most cautious of Germany's mostly pro-European politicians, accused the SPD of refusing to openly condemn "creative accounting" in assessing a member state's qualification for EMU.
In a television interview earlier on Friday, Stoiber accused France and Italy of cheating to meet the criteria.

Repeating his charge against the SPD, he said "I think it is a very, very bad situation that we would now accept this so-called creative accounting like the French and the Italians do it," he said. "We would then get a soft euro with higher interest rates and more unemployment.

"Then, we'll never succeed in having the Italians and the Spanish and the Portuguese (keep to) a strict application of the stability criteria. Then, the whole thing will start to slide, and I don't think the population would accept getting a softer euro in place of our hard deutschemark."
